deliveryStory.eyebrow: Glide · Notes from my one-person company
deliveryStory.title: Can Glide keep the right-click menu working?
deliveryStory.intro: I built Glide for Mac so you can hold the right mouse button and draw to move a window. A user found that the slightest wobble could make the browser menu disappear when all they wanted was a right-click.

steps.title: Work out what the person meant to do
steps.body: One mouse button can mean three things. Try a quick click, a slightly wobbly click and a deliberate stroke. The first two should open the menu. Only the third is meant to move a window.

steps.title: Give the click time to finish
steps.body: I made the trail appear once the mouse had moved far enough. Holding still can bring up hints. When you release the button, Glide checks for a direction or a loop. A quick click still opens the app’s menu even if your hand wobbled.

steps.title: Keep examples I can check again
steps.body: I turned those actions into automated checks and fixed the timing of the click sent back to the app. The fix appears in the public Glide 1.1.8 release notes alongside the Mac installers.

checks: Right-click with a slight wobble and no clear stroke
The menu opens where you clicked.
With the default global settings, hold the right button, draw upward and release

routes.body: Bring a screenshot or short recording with sensitive details removed. Show me where you get stuck and what you wanted to see. We can work through it on a 15-minute call.

report.question: How can a researcher check which report and passage an answer came from?
captions: Read the columns as separate sections of the same report.
Retrieve the matching passage together with its section heading.
Keep the citation with the answer so a reader can check it.

scan.question: How do you tell which heading a number belongs to after a table has been scanned?
captions: Spaces and line breaks alone do not identify a scanned table.
Use the position of each field to group it with the right column.
Keep the column headings so each row can be read on its own.

ledger.question: Which order does a payment belong to, and what should a reviewer see if the receipt is missing?
captions: Write a separate ledger entry for each transaction.
Match each payment receipt to its order and flag the missing one.
Keep the original order and the reason for review together.

tools.question: How does one tool pass its work to the next, and how can someone check the result?
captions: Break the task into reading the document and extracting the table.
Pass the output of the first tool into the second tool.
Keep inputs, calls and outputs together for review and replay.

reader.intro: Choose a case and follow the evidence through to the result.
reader.restored: This case has been restored to its starting state.

report.task: Check the claim that orders recovered
report.lead: The same news appears in a weekly report and a later digest. A researcher needs a passage that supports the claim as of a specific date.
report.decision: Retrieval identifies candidate passages. Dates and source quality inform their order. Retaining page references and layout positions lets a reviewer check whether a passage describes supply or demand.
report.check: Run the same question at the two different reporting dates. Verify that the evidence was public by each cutoff and follow the page reference to the passage. Measure retrieval and latency separately.
report.review: Keep the sources available to the researcher when only secondary coverage is available, or when reports disagree. A later summary adds no new survey evidence.

scan.task: Correct the boundary between units and quantities
scan.lead: A scan can recognize every character and still produce the wrong table. The second row is shifted to the right, pushing its unit into the quantity column.
scan.decision: Retain the positions of text on the source page, then check each reconstructed cell against the original tokens. Merged and empty cells flag areas to inspect. Every exported quantity must still belong to the right row and unit.
scan.check: Check each item, unit and quantity against its own source row. The project records describe a set of 50 difficult samples used for regression checks. This two-row example isolates the column-boundary problem.
scan.review: Merged cells, blank columns and missing values can distort downstream totals. Inspect character positions on the original page before releasing the extracted table.

ledger.task: Review the missing proof for order B
ledger.lead: An entry in the ledger still needs a matching payment document and receipt. Attaching the proof from a neighbouring order could make an open transaction appear settled.
ledger.decision: Keep the ledger, payment proof and incoming transfer record distinct and link them by order identifier. An exception stays with a reviewer, who can trace what was submitted and why it was accepted.
ledger.check: Trace the payment document and the incoming receipt back to their order identifiers. Check that the exception ticket references the same order. A neighbouring order’s proof is included to test that association.
ledger.review: Leave the order in review when proof is missing or points to another order. Keep a record of the attempt so the next reviewer can see why it failed.

tools.task: Find where the extraction run stopped
tools.lead: Reading a file successfully does not guarantee a usable table. The selected page and the handling of empty columns both affect the downstream result.
tools.decision: Inspect document reading, table extraction and validation separately. This example combines orchestration and table-audit techniques from several projects. Each rerun retains its own sample inputs and outputs.
tools.check: Record the input page, extraction rule, table dimensions and audit branch for each run. After a successful retry, inspect the original run to see which output blocked it.
tools.review: A page with no table calls for checking the input. A detail page with a blank column calls for checking extraction. Escalate the result for review if neither resolves it.

report.brief: Set the cutoff date, then check the source, passage and page.
report.question: How were orders trending as of the cutoff?
report.criteria: Use material published by the cutoff. Prefer the latest first-hand interviews and cite a passage about orders.

supply.text: Logistics delays continued to disrupt delivery of some materials.

demand.text: Interviewed factories reported flat new orders compared with the previous week, with no clear recovery.

supply.text: Key materials arrived more reliably, shortening the wait for production.

demand.text: Interviewed factories reported a recovery in new orders, driven mainly by repeat purchases.

supply.text: The digest quotes the March 6 weekly on delays in material deliveries.

demand.text: The digest quotes the flat orders reported in the March 6 interviews. It contains no new survey.

valid.title: Citation supported
valid.body: The passage discusses new orders directly and comes from the latest first-hand report available by the cutoff.

future.title: Not yet published by the cutoff
future.body: This would use future information. Choose an issue already published and check its demand passage.

section.title: This passage answers a supply question
section.body: Delivery times cannot establish whether orders recovered. Keep the document and select demand.

secondary.title: Later publication, older evidence
secondary.body: The digest repeats the March 6 interviews. Check the demand passage in the March 13 primary report.

outdated.title: A newer primary source was available
outdated.body: This passage does discuss orders, but it predates a later survey. Check the later issue.

scan.brief: In this fictional materials slip, the vertical rule is missing and the unit on the second row sits farther right. Move the column boundary, inspect both rows, then check the output.
scan.hint: Tokens left of the rule belong to the unit column. Tokens to its right belong to quantity. Use the slider or the arrow keys.
scan.missingUnit: Unit missing. Move the boundary right until the unit and number separate.
scan.missingQty: Quantity missing. Move the boundary left to return the number to its column.
scan.check: Check both rows and generate the table
scan.ready: Both rows are separated and ready to check.
scan.pending: An empty column still needs checking.

ledger.sample: Compare the payment proofs and receipts for the two orders, then log the missing evidence.
ledger.initialB: {B}: order recorded with no payment proof.
ledger.inspectA: The proof and the receipt refer to the same order.
ledger.inspectB: The order is recorded. Check which piece of evidence is missing.
ledger.requested: {B}: opened an exception for missing proof.
ledger.noProof: {B}: missing payment proof. Match not confirmed.
ledger.chosen: Sample selected. Attach it before verifying.
ledger.attachedA: {B}: candidate proof V-A attached for review.
ledger.attachedB: {B}: candidate proof V-B attached for review.
ledger.mismatch: V-A belongs to {A}. The exception for {B} stays open. Replace the proof and retry.
ledger.verified: {B}: V-B and receipt R-B refer to the same order. Review complete.

tools.brief: Count the pieces on slip IN-07 and inspect the inputs, outputs and validation for each run.
tools.cover: Use one row per batch. Count each item in pieces. The receiving log is on page 2.

reason.noTable: This page contains instructions. Choose page 2 for the receiving log, then run again.
reason.ghost: Column {col} has an empty heading and all {rows} of its data cells are blank. Compare the result with the receipt, then change the extraction rule.
reason.passed: Both batches have a batch ID and a piece count. The workflow can now send the counts to the summation step.

routes.noTable: Return to page selection. Total withheld.
routes.ghost: Return to table extraction. Total withheld.

plan.title: Run request
plan.rule: The page must contain data rows. If three or more columns are detected, reject any column whose heading and entries are all blank.
